1.pericope_label: Concerning spiritual gifts I would not have you ignorant

schools.summary: Chrysostom warns that this whole place is very obscure, but locates the obscurity in ourselves, in our ignorance of facts that then occurred and now take place no longer. Whoever was baptized straightway spake with tongues, and many prophesied; coming over from idols without clear knowledge or training in the ancient Scriptures, they received the Spirit at once upon baptism, and since the Spirit is invisible God gave some sensible proof of that energy — one speaking in the Persian, another in the Roman, another in the Indian, which made it manifest to those without that the Spirit was in the very person speaking. Most abundant of all was the gift of tongues, and it became a cause of division, not from its own nature but from the perverseness of those who had received it, the possessors of the greater gifts being lifted up against them that had the lesser, and these again envying the owners of the greater.

Gill observes that the word gifts is not in the original though rightly supplied, since the apostle means neither graces nor doctrines nor spiritual men, spiritual gifts being the subject of this chapter and the two following. Calvin states the purpose the argument will serve: the Corinthians abused God's gifts for ostentation and show while love was little regarded, so Paul shows for what purpose believers are adorned with them, namely the edification of their brethren. That God is their author he proves from their own experience, reminding them how ignorant and stupid they were, and destitute of all spiritual light, before God called them, whence it appears they were furnished not by nature but through his unmerited benignity.

Henry draws the distinction on which the whole chapter turns. Gifts and graces greatly differ: both are freely given of God, but grace is given for the salvation of those who have it, whereas gifts are bestowed for the advantage and salvation of others; and there may be great gifts where there is not a dram of grace, the persons possessed of them being utterly out of the divine favour. They are great instances of divine benignity, but do not of themselves prove those who have them objects of divine complacency, this church being rich in gifts while many things in it were scandalously out of order.

Clarke would as readily translate the words concerning spiritual persons as concerning spiritual gifts, and thinks the former agrees better with the context; what the apostle wishes them to know is whence such gifts come and for what end, that each may serve the church in the capacity God has placed him in, so that there be no schism in the body. Wesley notes that the abundance of these gifts in the churches of Greece refuted the idle learning of the Greek philosophers, though the Corinthians used them unwisely.

Robertson takes the opening formula for a sign that this was among the items asked about in the letter to Paul, introduced just as the problem of meats offered to idols had been, and that the question runs to the end of the fourteenth chapter. Ellicott sets the scene: in that early age the church was full of the divine energy of spiritual youth, and from the indwelling Spirit resulted marvellous gifts, some of which ceased with the apostolic age, some of which seem to have lingered for centuries, even to our own day, declaring themselves in times of profound religious awakening. Barnes finds the abuse to be one of precedency, those thus favoured claiming higher honour than the less distinguished, and answers that all filled important places, as the parts of the human system are necessary to its symmetry and health.

debates.question: Is the subject spiritual gifts or spiritual persons?

positions.position: gifts — the word is not in the original but is rightly supplied, since spiritual gifts are the subject of this chapter and the two following
spiritual persons might as readily be translated, and agrees better with the context

themes: now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant
gifts and graces distinguished
why the gifts were given

2.pericope_label: Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols

schools.summary: Gill takes the word Gentiles here of religion rather than nation, the Syriac rendering it profane, and observes that it must be understood of one part of the church only, since some were Jews; the apostle notes it to humble them, so that if they were now favoured with any of the Spirit's gifts these must be owing to grace and not to their deserts. Calvin draws the doctrine out of the experience: we must be directed by the Spirit of God or we shall wander on for ever, and it follows that all things pertaining to the true knowledge of God are gifts of the Holy Spirit. He raises the objection himself, that the wicked sometimes speak of Christ in honourable and magnificent terms, and answers that they undoubtedly have the Spirit so far as that effect goes, but that the gift of regeneration is one thing and the gift of bare intelligence, with which Judas was endowed when he preached the gospel, quite another.

Clarke says they were hurried by their passions into a senseless worship calculated only to gratify animal propensities, and that the dumbness was double, since not only could the image not speak but neither could the god or demon it pretended to represent — a full proof that an idol is nothing in the world. On the rule that follows he observes that it was granted on all hands that there could be no religion without divine inspiration, and that since the Spirit through all the law and the prophets gave testimony to the Messiah, no man under that inspiration could say to him anathema, as the Jews did. Wesley puts the first clause in a phrase, the blind carried away to the dumb, and that by the subtlety of their priests, and reduces the whole to a sum: none have the Holy Spirit but Christians, and all Christians have him.

Ellicott finds the argument to lie in a comparison of miracles: so far from tongues and prophesying being the most wonderful, the greatest of all was their own conversion, since that blind followers of dumb idols should be transformed into intelligent believers in the living Word was the most striking work of the Spirit. Barnes generalises sharply, that no system of paganism consults the freedom and independence of the mind of man, being everywhere a system of power and not of thought; and he is careful about the rule that follows, the meaning being not that no one has the physical ability to say Jesus is Lord, since all men can say this, but that none will be heartily disposed to say it unless brought to that state by the Spirit. Robertson hears in the confession a challenge to the empire, the word for Lord being common in the Greek Old Testament for God and used freely by the Romans of the emperor in his worship; he recalls the demand made of Polycarp that he say Caesar is Lord, and how each time he answered Jesus is Lord, paying for his loyalty with his life.

outliers.note: Concludes from the rule that since the Jews said anathema to Jesus, they were no longer under the Spirit's inspiration.

themes: ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols
no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed
no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost

4.pericope_label: Diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit

schools.summary: Gill reads the diversity as a rebuke to both parties at once: the gifts spring from the free grace and good pleasure of God, not from the merits of men, so that those with the largest share should not boast of them as acquired by themselves, and those with the smallest should be content and thankful, for though the gifts differ and none have all, yet all have some. Calvin puts the matter as a question of proportion. The symmetry of the Church consists of a manifold unity, when the variety of gifts is directed to one object, as in music there are different sounds yet suited to each other with such adaptation as to produce concord. He sets this passage beside the twelfth of Romans and finds the two doing opposite work: there every one is ordered to be content with his own gifts and cultivate the department assigned him; here every one is ordered to bring what he has to the common heap, not keeping back God's gifts so as to enjoy them apart.

Clarke defines the gifts as gracious endowments leading to miraculous results by the extraordinary influences of the Holy Spirit, and on the second clause lists the offices — apostle, prophet and teacher, under which were probably included bishop, pastor and deacon — the qualifications and the appointments alike coming immediately from the one Lord Jesus Christ. Wesley states the relation of the three verses in a figure: divers streams, but all from one fountain, this verse speaking of the Holy Ghost, the next of Christ, the sixth of God the Father.

Robertson notes that the word rendered diversities is an old term for distinctions or distributions, found only here in the New Testament, and that the word for gift means a favour bestowed without any merit. Barnes draws out what the repetition is for: since all these endowments are produced by the same Spirit, have the same divine origin, and answer some important purpose in the church, none is to be despised, nor any man authorised to treat another with contempt, the Spirit having divided and conferred them according to his sovereign will. The same follows for the offices, since all had their appointment from Christ and all are necessary, so that none should be proud of an elevated station nor depressed at being designated to a humbler one.

outliers.note: Defends the plain sense of the word Spirit against the German critics, at whose head he places Eichhorn, who would take it to mean nature, the same natural endowments cultivated in various measures by art and education; that reading makes manifest nonsense and destroys the concinnity of the three verses.
Marks a further use of the passage against those who think the name Spirit means nothing essential but merely the gifts or actions of divine power.

themes: now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit
differences of administrations, but the same Lord
diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all

7.pericope_label: The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal

schools.summary: Gill turns the phrase round: it is not that which the Spirit manifests, such as the grace of God or the doctrines of the gospel, but that which shows that a man has the Spirit, the gifts being such as declare their author. Calvin says the apostle points out the purpose for which God has appointed his gifts, since he does not confer them in vain nor intend them to serve the purpose of ostentation. He allows the word two senses, passive and active, and prefers the active: the Spirit, when he enriches us with any gift, unlocks his treasures to bring out things that would otherwise have been concealed and shut up. A third view he rejects as harsh and forced, that the term is used because unbelievers recognise God only by visible miracles.

Clarke reports that the fathers render the word variously, by illumination, by demonstration, by operation, and takes the apostle's meaning to be that whatever gifts God has bestowed, and in whatever ways the Spirit may have shown himself, it is all for the common benefit of the church, God having given no gift to any man for his own private advantage. On the first item of the list he would render the leading word not word but doctrine, as in many other places of the New Testament, and takes the doctrine of wisdom for the mystery of our redemption, in which the wisdom of God was most eminently conspicuous. Wesley states the verse in a line: the gift whereby the Spirit manifests itself, given to each for the profit of the whole body.

Barnes takes the word for that which makes anything conspicuous or plain, as conduct manifests the state of the heart, and is careful about the reach of the every man: the apostle is discoursing only of Christians, and the verse is very improperly adduced to prove that the gifts of the Spirit are conferred alike on all men, or that pagans and blasphemers are under his enlightening influences. He warns also against reading the list that follows as a ranking, since the design seems not to observe the order of value but to state, as it occurred to him, that these various endowments had been conferred on different men. Ellicott presses the word itself to the same end as the others: if the gift were only for a man's own benefit it would cease to be a showing forth at all, since it would be enough to possess the Spirit consciously to oneself, but the object of light is to give light to others. Robertson notes that the word is late, occurring in the New Testament only here and in the second epistle to Corinth.

debates.question: What is the manifestation of the Spirit?

positions.position: not what the Spirit manifests, but what shows that a man has the Spirit
that which makes anything conspicuous or plain, as conduct manifests the state of the heart
active rather than passive — the Spirit unlocks his treasures and brings out what would otherwise have been shut up

themes: the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal
to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom
to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit

9.pericope_label: To another faith, to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit

schools.summary: Gill would rather have the faith here named the doctrine of faith, with ability to preach it and boldness to defend it in the face of all opposition, given more or less to pastors and teachers, though he grants it is generally understood of a faith of working miracles. He reports a second reading of the working of miracles, that some understand the extraordinary powers the apostles had of punishing offenders, instancing Peter striking Ananias and Sapphira dead, Paul smiting Elymas with blindness, and the delivering of the incestuous person to Satan. Calvin draws the conclusion the list has been building toward: those act amiss who, having no concern for participation, break asunder that holy harmony which is fitly adjusted only when, under the guidance of the same Spirit, all conspire toward one object. To no one does the Spirit give all, lest any, satisfied with his own portion, should separate himself from the rest and live solely for himself. And since will is here ascribed to the Spirit, and that in connection with power, Calvin concludes the Spirit to be truly and properly God.

Wesley takes the faith for an extraordinary trust in God under the most dangerous circumstances, and will not confine the gift of healing to its most conspicuous form, since it may exert itself also, though in a lower degree, where natural remedies are applied. He notes too that the words as he will imply not so much arbitrary pleasure as a determination founded on wise counsel. Clarke observes that all these gifts were miraculously bestowed and could not be acquired by human art, the different languages excepted, and that even these were given in such circumstances as sufficiently proved them miraculous also.

Ellicott says the faith cannot mean the faith necessary to salvation, since that belongs to all Christians, and warns that prophecy is not to be taken in its modern limited sense of foretelling the future but of forthtelling truth generally. Robertson calls the faith not the faith of surrender but wonder-working faith, and calls the discerning of spirits a most needed gift, to tell whether the gifts were really of the Holy Spirit — or the so-called gifts of today — or merely strange though natural, or even diabolical. Barnes uses the word faith to praise a quality he thinks undervalued: many of the most useful men in the church are distinguished mainly for their simple confidence in God's promises, and often accomplish more by prayer and faith than others distinguished for wisdom and learning; perhaps it is despised by many because it may be obtained by all. On the discerning of spirits he explains the need, since where the gift of prophecy conferred such advantages there would be many pretenders to it.

positions.position: not saving faith, which belongs to all Christians, but wonder-working faith, an extraordinary trust in God under the most dangerous circumstances
rather the doctrine of faith, with ability to preach it and boldness to defend it, though it is generally understood of a faith of working miracles

outliers.note: Extends the gift of healing to natural remedies, and thinks it may often be this, and not superior skill, that makes some physicians more successful than others; as after the golden shields were lost the king of Judah put brazen ones in their place, so the power of God now exerts itself in a more covert manner.

themes: to another faith by the same Spirit
to another the gifts of healing, to another the working of miracles
dividing to every man severally as he will

12.pericope_label: As the body is one and hath many members, so also is Christ

schools.summary: Chrysostom notices the apostle's habit of reasoning from nature, as when he asked whether nature does not teach that long hair is a dishonour to a man and a glory to a woman, and when, forbidding the idol-sacrifices, he drew his arguments from the Olympic games, from shepherds and soldiers and husbandmen. Here he brings forward another common example, by which he fights hard to prove that no one was really put in a worse condition, a thing marvellous to be able to demonstrate and calculated to refresh the weaker sort. For nothing so consoles the person of small spirit and inferior gifts, Chrysostom says, or so persuades him not to grieve, as being convinced that he is not left with less than his share.

Gill states the ground plainly, that a human body is but one, and not more. Calvin recalls that Menenius Agrippa, when he wished to conciliate the Roman people at variance with the senate, made use of an apologue not very unlike the doctrine of Paul here; and he adds that the gifts were not conferred in order that every one should enjoy his own separately, but that one should help another.

Henry expounds the similitude at length. Christ and his church make one body, as head and limbs, made up of many parts yet but one, since all are baptized into it and made to drink of the same Spirit, Jews and Gentiles, bond and free, being upon a level in this. Christians are enrolled by baptism, the outward rite being of divine institution and significant of the new birth; but it is by the renewing of the Holy Ghost that we are grafted in, and not merely by drinking the wine at the other ordinance but by drinking into one Spirit that we are maintained in union. He then turns it to the comfort of the least: the lowliest member makes a part of the whole, and though the foot and the ear are less useful, perhaps, than the hand and the eye, they do not cease to belong to it, so that the meanest in Christ's body stands as truly there as the noblest and is as dearly cherished. And the variety is not a defect but a beauty, for what a monster would a frame be if it were all ear, or eye, or arm.

Clarke fills out the figure — though the human frame has many members and a great variety of parts, it is yet one entire system, every part being requisite to the completeness of the whole — and observes on the second clause that it cannot be supposed Christ is composed of many members, so that the term Church must be supplied, unless, which he thinks not improbable, the name Christ is here used to express the church, or whole company of Christian believers.

Barnes reaches the same clause by a figure of speech: as the head is the most important part it may stand for the whole, and the name Christ, the head of the church, is here put for the whole of which he is head, a figure common in all languages. Robertson grants that one would naturally expect the apostle to say, so also is the body of Christ, and notes that Aristotle had used the word body of the state, the body politic; what Paul means is that Christ as head has a body composed of members with varied gifts and functions, like the parts of the human frame, all vitally joined to the head and to each other.

debates.question: Why does the apostle say so also is Christ, rather than the body of Christ?

positions.position: the term Church must be supplied, unless the name Christ is here used to express the church itself, the whole company of Christian believers
a figure of speech common in all languages, the head standing for the whole of which he is head
Christ as head has a body composed of members with varied gifts and functions, all vitally joined to the head and to each other

themes: as the body is one, and hath many members
all the members of that one body, being many, are one body
so also is Christ

13.pericope_label: By one Spirit are we all baptized into one body

schools.summary: Gill denies flatly that water is intended, since the apostle says not in one and the same water but by one Spirit; not all who are washed are baptized by the Spirit, as the case of Simon Magus shows, and the outward rite does not of itself incorporate anyone into the church, seeing that persons may receive it and yet never be joined to one. There is an allusion to it, he grants, but what is intended is the grace of the Spirit in regeneration and sanctification. Calvin takes it rather as a proof drawn from the effect of the rite: we are by it engrafted into Christ's body, bound together as members by a mutual link and living one life, so that every one who would remain in the church must cultivate this fellowship. He speaks, however, of the washing of believers, efficacious through the grace of the Spirit, for in many it is merely in the letter, the symbol without the reality. On the drinking he thinks the apostle intended an allusion to the Supper, since there is no correspondence between drinking and washing, whereas in that ordinance we drink of the life-giving blood of Christ that we may have life in common with him.

Clarke draws the comparison out through the soul: as the body of man, though composed of many members, is informed and influenced by one soul, so the church of Christ, which is his body, is informed and influenced by one Spirit, the Holy Ghost actuating and working by his spiritual frame as the human soul does in ours. On the drinking he understands a being made partakers of the gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost, agreeably to the words of our Lord, that if any man thirst he should come and drink. Wesley marks how far apart the pairs stand, Jews and Gentiles at the greatest distance by nature, slaves and freemen at the greatest distance by law and custom, and yet all united in one body; and he combines the two readings of the last clause, that in that cup, received by faith, we all imbibed one Spirit, who first inspired and still preserves the life of God in our souls.

Barnes agrees that the connexion seems rather to require the baptism of the Holy Ghost, though he reports that Bloomfield, Calvin and Doddridge understand the ordinance, in which case the sense would be that by the very profession then made they had all become members of one and the same body. He lingers on the second pair of terms: religion conferred no favours on the free which it did not confer on the bondman, and this would tend to secure their proper treatment more than anything else could, while increasing rather than diminishing their real respect for their masters. On the drinking he thinks it probably refers to their partaking together of the cup in the Lord's Supper. Ellicott would render the clause not to drink into but simply to drink one Spirit, and takes the rite to have been not only a watering of the convert with the washing of regeneration but a partaking of one Spirit on his part, the verb being that used where Apollos watered. Robertson reads the baptism of a definite past event in the life of each, of whatever race or class, when they put on the outward badge of service to Christ, the token of an inward change already wrought.

debates.question: Is the baptism here the outward rite or the baptism of the Spirit?

positions.position: not water at all — the grace of the Spirit in regeneration and sanctification, since the outward rite does not of itself incorporate anyone into the church
the connexion seems rather to require the baptism of the Holy Ghost, though others understand the ordinance
the rite itself, but as the washing of believers, efficacious through the grace of the Spirit and in many merely in the letter
a definite past event in the life of each, when they put on the outward badge of service to Christ, the token of an inward change already wrought

debates.question: What is it to be made to drink into one Spirit?

positions.position: a partaking together of the cup in the Lord’s Supper, drinking of the life-giving blood of Christ that we may have life in common with him
simply to drink one Spirit — the convert not only watered with the washing of regeneration but himself partaking of one Spirit
a being made partakers of the gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost, as our Lord bade the thirsty come and drink

themes: by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body
whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free
have been all made to drink into one Spirit

14.pericope_label: If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body

schools.summary: Gill gives the foot its dignity: it is the lowest member, nearest the earth, treading upon it, sustaining the whole weight of the body and performing the more drudging exercises of standing and walking, and may represent one in the lowest station in the church, a doorkeeper in the house of God, with the smallest degree of heavenly affection and spiritual light. Calvin presses the absurdity of the supposed revolt. Each member ought to rest satisfied with its own place and not envy the others; if our hands were, from envy, to refuse to discharge their office, would nature endure it, and would the hand be listened to when wishing to be separated from the body? These things are said of the natural body, Calvin adds, but must be applied to the Church, lest ambition or misdirected emulation lead one who occupies an inferior station to grudge his services to those above him.

Clarke states the dependence plainly: as all the members of the body depend on each other and minister to the general support of the system, so in the church the private members are intimately connected among themselves and with their pastors, without which union no church can subsist. Wesley notices whom each complainant is made to envy — the foot elegantly introduced as speaking of the hand, and the ear of the eye, each of a part that has some resemblance to it, so that among men each is apt to compare himself with those whose gifts resemble his own rather than with those at a distance. He offers a reading of the four: perhaps the foot represents private Christians, the hand officers in the church, the eye teachers, the ear hearers.

Robertson allows that the opening statement sounds like a truism but calls it the key to the whole problem of church life, local and general, and notes that the parable behind it was an old one, Socrates having asked how absurd it would be if feet and hands worked against one another when God made them to co-operate, while Seneca and Marcus Aurelius allude to it too; his short answer to the complaint is that thinking or saying so does not change the fact. Barnes tells the best-known version at length, the apologue used by Menenius Agrippa, as Livy relates, to repress a rebellion raised against the nobles as useless and cumbersome to the state: he represented the members as conspiring against the stomach on the ground that it was inactive and consumed everything, and showed that the consequence was a universal wasting away of the whole frame for want of the nutriment the stomach supplied. Ellicott finds the same idea turned into verse by Pope, and states the principle behind it, that it would be as absurd for the body to be one member as for the members to lose their individuality, since there is a corporate body composed of divers members — the difference between a dead machine and a living organism.

themes: if the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body
if the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing?
the members of one body are not therefore not of the body

18.pericope_label: But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him

schools.summary: Gill notes that the members of a natural body, as they are made and fashioned by God in the form they have, are each also set by him in the place they occupy, and observes that they are of different make and shape, in different parts and places, and of different use and service. Calvin makes the appointment itself the argument: it has pleased God that the body should consist of various members endowed with various offices and gifts, and that member therefore which will not rest satisfied with its own station will wage war with God after the manner of the giants. He gives the reason behind the arrangement, that God has not acted at random in assigning different gifts, but because it was necessary for the preservation of the body, since if this symmetry were taken away there would be utter confusion; and he presses the apostle's word, which he takes for a mass all of one shape, not distinguished by any variety, such that if God were to fashion our body into a mass of that kind it would be a useless heap. Calvin finds the stress of the whole question to lie here: the unity of the body is of such a nature as cannot be maintained but by a diversity of members.

Wesley adds only that it pleased him with the most exquisite wisdom and goodness, and draws from the unity of the body what he takes to be its necessary consequence, that the several members need one another.

Barnes puts the reason: God has formed the body, with its various members, as he saw would best conduce to the harmony and usefulness of all; and on the supposition that all were one member he states the consequence flatly, that if there were nothing but an eye, an ear or a limb there would be no body at all, just as the church could not exist if there were none but apostles, or none but prophets and teachers. Robertson reads the opening words as marking the turn of the argument, but now, as things actually are, in contrast to that absurdity, and observes that the verb is middle, so that God did it, and of himself; why then, he asks, challenge God's will? He calls the closing clause the argument in a nutshell, in a single epigram: many members, but one body. Ellicott marks the turn from the argument to the fact, the apostle coming from the reduction to absurdity to things as they are and stating a mutual interdependence among the members, the eye dependent on the hand and the head upon the feet; the illustration is drawn out in this direction, he suggests, to rebuke those who, possessing what were reckoned the important spiritual gifts, despised those the Spirit had bestowed on others.

themes: God hath set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him
if they were all one member, where were the body?
now are they many members, yet but one body

21.pericope_label: The eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee

schools.summary: Chrysostom marks the turn in the argument. Having checked the envy of those in lower rank, and taken off the dejection they were likely to feel because richer endowments had been vouchsafed to others, the apostle now humbles the pride of the highly favoured; for though a gift be smaller it is necessary, and as when the one is absent many functions are impeded, so without the other there is a maim in the fulness of the Church. He presses the exact words: the apostle said not, will not say, but cannot say, so that even should the eye wish to and actually pronounce the sentence, the thing remains out of the question and inconsistent with nature. He notices too the choice of instances, that Paul seizes the two extremes and tries his argument first on the hand and the eye, then on the head and the feet, so adding force to the example.

Calvin sets the two halves of the exhortation side by side. Hitherto the apostle has shown what belongs to the office of the humbler members, to discharge their duty toward the whole and not grudge the more distinguished their eminence; now, turning about, he lays it upon the honoured not to look down on those beneath, whom they cannot do without. The eye excels the hand and yet may neither scorn it nor insult over it as a thing superfluous; the argument Calvin traces here is drawn from usefulness, that whatever ranks lowest in general esteem proves the more indispensable. He supplies the reason for the covering of the uncomely: the dishonour of a single member turns out to the common disgrace of the whole body, and that is why we take such pains to cover what would shame us if seen. Gill observes that the apostle advances by a beautiful gradation, singling out the portions which are weaker, less creditable and less comely, and demonstrating how needful they are.

Clarke identifies the feebler members with the principal viscera — heart, lungs, stomach and intestinal canal. A man may lose an eye by accident, an arm or a leg may be amputated, and he lives and remains vigorous; let stomach, heart or lungs be taken away and life becomes necessarily extinct. Hence such organs are not merely covered, but the cavities lodging them are girded about and fortified for their defence, since upon their proper working life so immediately depends.

Robertson compresses the whole into a phrase, that the superior organs need the inferior ones, and notes that the verb for bestowing honour means literally to place around, as one puts on a garland or a garment, while a word for gracefulness found nowhere else in the New Testament carries the point. Barnes turns the anatomy upon the church and reckons the thought a beautiful one: those members most retiring and feeble in appearance, hidden from public view, unnoticed and unknown — the lowly, the meek, the peaceable and the prayerful — are often more requisite to her true welfare than any celebrated for talent and learning, so that she can better spare many a man, even in the ministry, who is learned and eloquent and popular, than some obscure Christian who is to her what the heart and the lungs are to the life. He explains that the abundant honour spoken of is precisely a matter of apparel, since what decency bids us conceal we not only cover but study to adorn, while the comely face is left bare. Ellicott adds the plain sense of the clause, that the parts reckoned less seemly are the more abundantly cared for, being carefully clothed, as distinguished from the face and hands, which go uncovered.

themes: the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee
those members of the body which seem to be more feeble are necessary
upon these we bestow more abundant honour

24.pericope_label: God hath tempered the body together, that there should be no schism in the body

schools.summary: Gill takes the comely parts to be face, eyes, nose, lips and cheeks, which want no external covering nor any borrowed ornament; and so, he adds, those eminent for grace and holiness, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience, need no such veil as the others to hide them from the world. Calvin sees the point of an earlier verse repeated more explicitly. God has appointed this symmetry with a view to the advantage of the whole, since on no other terms can it keep its footing. Whence comes it that every member is spontaneously concerned for the honour of a less comely one, and that all agree to conceal its shame? The inclination was implanted by God, for without it the frame would quickly fly apart; and where anyone assumes more than belongs to him, Calvin warns, the body is not merely shattered and the order of nature perverted, but the authority of God is openly set at naught. On the sympathy he adds that nothing so promotes harmony as this community of interest, when each feels himself enriched by the prosperity of others and impoverished by their want.

Wesley states the honour plainly, that the lacking part is cared for and served by the noblest. Clarke presses the mutual watchfulness: so completely has God tempered the whole that not the smallest visible part can be removed without injuring the proportions and producing deformity; the eyes and ears keep guard for the general safety, set in the head like sentinels in a tower to perceive the first approach of a foe. He adds that whatever adorns or strengthens any single part gives a general pleasure to the whole man.

Ellicott begins with the punctuation, that the clause about our comely parts closes the previous sentence and a new one opens at But God hath tempered, where the ordinary practice of covering the body is shown to agree with God's evident intention; and he observes that the Corinthians turned their differences of gifts into an occasion of schism, exalting some and depreciating others, when the variety was designed to breed a mutual dependence that promotes unity. Barnes reads the verb literally as mingled, God having made the parts coalesce and formed a strict union; and he will not have the sympathy reckoned a mere feeling, since a disease left unarrested is carried by the blood through every part until life is destroyed, so that the injury of one is by natural connexion the injury of all. Hence when one is tempted or afflicted the rest should bear one another's burdens, and when a member is raised to a station of influence the benefit is common property, which ought to repress envy at another's elevation. Robertson finds the word for tempering rarer than Barnes allows: Plato had used this very verb of the way God compounded the elements in creating soul and body, and Paul, borrowing it, rejects the notion that matter is evil and the organs degrading. He notes that the word for suffering together is a medical term in Hippocrates and Galen, and that Plato had said the body politic feels the hurt as the whole man feels a hurt finger.

themes: God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked
that there should be no schism in the body
whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it

27.pericope_label: Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular

schools.summary: Chrysostom anticipates the objection: what is the example of the body to us, since the body is a slave to nature while our good deeds are of choice? The apostle therefore turns the figure upon their own concerns, signifying that we ought to have from deliberate agreement the same concord of design that the limbs have from nature; and if our body ought not to be divided, much less Christ's, and less by as much as grace is mightier than nature. He then presses the added word, severally. Since the whole body was not the Corinthian church but the church in every part of the world, the apostle qualifies his phrase: the church among you is one portion of that body which is made up of all the churches, so that you must be at peace not with yourselves alone but with the whole church throughout the world.

Gill guards the term against mistake: this is not Christ's natural body, which the Father prepared for him and in which he bore our sins on the tree, offered up once for all, nor his sacramental body, the bread in the supper which represents it, but his body mystical, the church; nor were the Corinthians that whole body, only a part, as every congregation is a part of the church universal. Calvin closes on the practical note: what any man has was given him for his brethren's edification, and must be brought forward rather than buried within himself or used as his own. Let the richly endowed not swell with pride, since nothing is so slight as to be useless, the least of the pious bearing fruit according to his slender capacity; and let the lowlier neither envy those above them nor withhold their duty. Calvin thinks Chrysostom's reading of the word severally forced, and prefers to refer the phrase back to the division of members already made, so that each is a member according as his portion and definite work have been assigned him.

Henry draws the practical inference. Each is a member of the body, not the body; each depends upon the rest and owes them care and concern. Mutual indifference, therefore, and much more contempt and hatred and envy and strife, are things unnatural in Christians, as unnatural as limbs of one frame having no regard for each other, or quarrelling among themselves. This, Henry says, is the whole scope of the argument: to put down the proud, vaunting and contentious spirit that their spiritual gifts had raised among the Corinthians.

Clarke applies it to the ministry. Every member is meant to be subservient to the rest, to mourn and rejoice with them, and each is necessary to the beauty, proportion, strength and perfection of the whole, not one useless, not one superfluous. Paul, Apollos and Cephas, with all their variety of gifts, serve alike for the perfecting of the saints; hence no teacher should be exalted above another or set against him. As the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee, so luminous Apollos cannot say to laborious Paul, I can build up and preserve the church without thee. Clarke grants that fancy might match particular ministers to particular limbs, but judges such matching no part of the apostle's plan. Wesley says in a breath what Gill says at length, that they are the body and members of Christ, part of them and not the whole.

Ellicott marks the place of the verse: here the foregoing illustration is applied in general terms, its detailed application following immediately after. Barnes keeps the anatomy in view, that as all the limbs compose one frame under a common head, so Christ presides over the whole. Robertson gives the added word its plain force, that each has his own place and function.

debates.question: What does the word severally add?

positions.position: it qualifies the phrase, since the whole body was not the Corinthian church but the church in every part of the world
that reading is forced; the phrase refers back to the division of members already made, each being a member as his portion and definite work have been assigned him
simply that each has his own place and function in the body of Christ

themes: now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular
the church among you is a part of the church everywhere
what any man has was given him for his brethren

28.pericope_label: God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers

schools.summary: Gill notes that the apostle, having given the various gifts of the Spirit which qualify men for service, here enumerates the several offices and officers themselves. Calvin fixes on the order and thinks it should be carefully observed: the Lord never appointed ministers without first endowing them with the requisite gifts, the natural order being that gifts come before the office to be discharged. From this he draws a sharp inference, that those are fanatics, and actuated by an evil spirit, who thrust themselves into the church while destitute of the necessary qualifications, boasting that they are under the Spirit's influence and glorying in a secret call from God while remaining unlearned and utterly ignorant. He also divides the list: some offices named are perpetual, being necessary for the government of the church; others were temporary, appointed at the outset for founding it and ceasing shortly after. To the second class belongs the apostleship, since the Lord assigned the apostles no fixed limits or parishes but sent them as ambassadors among all nations, whereas a pastor must take care of the flock committed to his charge. By prophet Calvin understands not one who predicts, but an eminent interpreter of Scripture endowed with uncommon wisdom in discerning the present necessity of the church.

Clarke sees here the same evident distinctions God has made among the members of the human frame, and unfolds each title from its roots: an apostle is one sent from place to place, designated immediately by Christ; a prophet one who speaks beforehand, predicting things to come under divine inspiration, though the word is often applied to any who preach the gospel; a teacher instructs the people in the elements of religion. He takes helps as the apostles' assistants, who baptized converts and went where they could not, the Levites being called helps of the priests; and he denies that governments means ruling power at all, taking it for a deep comprehensive mind, profoundly wise and prudent. Wesley sharpens the list: apostles plant the gospel among the heathen; prophets either foretell what is coming or speak by extraordinary inspiration; teachers precede even those who work miracles, and under these heads the evangelists and pastors of Ephesians are comprised. He holds that helps and governments are not distinct offices at all.

Barnes reads the verb strictly, that God has appointed, constituted, ordained these various ranks, the sequence marking honour and endowment: the apostles stand first, holding the highest authority and most signally qualified, prophets second in point of gifts, teachers third. He notes that the word for helps occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means aid or those who render it, perhaps the care of the poor and sick and orphans, perhaps those who attended the apostles as Priscilla and Aquila did, while governments comes from steering a ship; and he holds that no permanent offices are established here. Robertson watches the sentence break its own shape, since Paul begins as though he would say some apostles, some prophets, then abandons the construction for first, second, then, and at miracles shifts from the concrete to the abstract. Prophets, he says, are forth-speakers for God, still needed if men will let the Spirit move them to utter the deep things of God; and it is a calamity when a preacher is no longer a teacher but only an exhorter. He guesses deacons for helps and bishops or elders for governments, and remarks the curiosity that these two offices, never specifically named, are the two that have survived.

debates.question: What are the helps and the governments?

positions.position: probably the deacons for the one, and bishops or elders for the other — curiously, the two offices never specifically named are the two that survive
aid of some kind, perhaps the care of the poor and sick, perhaps those who attended the apostles; and governments from the steering of a ship, but no permanent office is established here
the apostles’ own assistants, who baptized their converts; and governments not ruling power at all, but a deep and comprehensive mind
not distinct offices — any might be called helps from a dexterity in helping the distressed, and governments from a talent for presiding

outliers.note: Calls those fanatics, and actuated by an evil spirit, who thrust themselves into the church destitute of the necessary qualifications, glorying in a secret call from God while unlearned and utterly ignorant.

themes: God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers
after that miracles, then gifts of healings
helps, governments, diversities of tongues

29.pericope_label: Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers?

schools.summary: Gill answers the questions bluntly: no, some are prophets as distinct from apostles, some are teachers as distinct from both, and some are neither. On the gifts of healing he adds a practical instance, that when such gifts were still in being they were not common property, the anointing with oil for the recovery of the sick being performed by the elders of the church and not by its ordinary members, the sick being required to send for them. Calvin heads off a misreading before drawing his conclusion: it may well have happened that one man was endowed with many gifts and sustained two of the offices enumerated, and there is no inconsistency in that. But the apostle's design is twofold, to show first that no one possesses such fulness in everything as to have a sufficiency within himself, and second that offices no less than gifts are so distributed that no single member constitutes the whole. And Calvin names what all this is meant to destroy: Paul means to take away every occasion of proud boasting, of base envyings, of haughtiness and contempt of the brethren, of malignity and ambition.

Clarke reads the whole series the same way — all are not apostles, all are not prophets — and finds in it the settled method of God, who has distributed his various gifts among various persons, each of whom is needed for the complete edification of the body of Christ.

Robertson notes that the Greek particle heading each question expects a negative answer from every group in turn, and observes a small irregularity at the close, since the question about interpreting is added here to the catalogue given a verse or two earlier, though it did stand in the fuller list near the beginning of the chapter. Barnes will not let the questions be softened into a wish: they imply, with strong emphasis, that there could not be and ought not to be an even distribution of endowment, and it was simply not the case that all were equal or that all were qualified for the offices others actually filled. Whether a man approves the arrangement or not, it remains a plain matter of fact that some were fitted for the apostolic office and others were not, some furnished with prophetic gifts and others not.

themes: are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers?
have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues?
do all interpret?

31.pericope_label: Covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way

schools.summary: Gill lays out the three possible readings — as an assertion, ye do covet earnestly the best gifts, but I can show you something better; as a question, do ye zealously affect them and emulate one another in pursuit of them; or, as the translators have it, as an exhortation. He takes the best gifts to be not the highest and most extraordinary of those named but the most useful and beneficial to the church, preaching above the rest; for the Corinthians seemed most desirous of speaking with different tongues, yet the apostle proves at length that prophesying is preferable, as more serviceable and therefore more eligible. Calvin holds the difference between the readings slight as to the sense, and diagnoses the same fault: they aimed at show rather than usefulness, so that prophecy was neglected while languages sounded forth among them with great display and little profit. He is careful to add that Paul is not addressing individuals, as though wishing every man to aspire to prophecy or the teaching office, but recommending a general desire to promote edification.

Clarke inclines to the affirmative reading, and thinks it likely, since there were certainly more contentions at Corinth about the gifts than about the graces of the Spirit. He gives the warning underneath the verse: a man may possess the best of all these gifts and still be deficient in what is essential to his salvation, if he is without that love. Wesley simply reads it as an assertion — ye covet earnestly the best gifts, and they are worth your pursuit, though few of you can attain them — and says the same as Clarke of what follows, that here is a gift which all may, yea must, attain or perish.

Barnes reports the weight of opinion for the indicative. Doddridge urged that it would be a contradiction, after showing that these gifts are not at their own option and that no one ought to aspire above another, to undo the whole argument by inviting such rivalry; Locke and Macknight agreed, and the Syriac renders it, because you are zealous of the best gifts I will show you a more excellent way, while Grotius preferred a third sense, that they should pray God for the most useful endowments. Barnes nevertheless keeps the imperative, judging that the connection demands it, and admires the skill of the turn that follows: the apostle did not denounce their zeal as wicked, nor say it was wrong to desire high endowments, but regulated the impulse by setting before them an endowment more valuable than all the rest, open to everyone, and such that in the very proportion it was gained it would quiet discontent and strife and ambition. Ellicott insists the argument is not meant to check ardour or damp enthusiasm, since the Spirit wills to give each the best gift that each desires and is capable of receiving, so that receptivity, born of earnest and practical desire, is the determining cause in every case; and he adds that the more excellent way is not some gift to be sought instead of the others, but a more excellent manner of seeking them all. Robertson notes that the apostle unhesitatingly ranks some spiritual gifts above others, that the verb for zeal carries here its good sense and not the envy it bears elsewhere, and that the closing phrase is superlative rather than comparative, a way beyond all comparison; the chapter division here is poor, for the sentence belongs with what follows.

debates.question: Is the clause an exhortation or a statement of what they were already doing?

positions.position: an exhortation — the connection demands the imperative, though Doddridge, Locke, Macknight and the Syriac read it as a statement
the affirmative reading is likely, since there were more contentions at Corinth about the gifts than about the graces
it may be rendered as assertion, question or exhortation
the difference is slight as to the sense

and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way
that more excellent way is love
